title: The Great Rupert

evidence.note: Wikipedia states the film entered the public domain in 1978 when its 28-year copyright term lapsed without renewal. That is a secondary claim. No Catalog of Copyright Entries renewal page or Copyright Office record was read in this session, so non-renewal is not established here. Stanford's Copyright Renewal Database covers book renewals, not films, so it is not a usable source for this film's print status; a search of it for "Great Rupert" returned no results regardless. The Copyright Office public catalog could not be queried non-interactively. The Internet Archive item carries a Public Domain Mark 1.0 tag, which is an uploader label and not a rights record.

The recorded soundtrack of a sound film normally shares the film's own copyright status, so the score likely follows the print. Neither the print nor any separate score registration or renewal has been verified.

Wikipedia and the Internet Archive item description say the film is based on a story by Ted Allan that was also published as a children's book, Willie the Squowse. Neither page gives the book's publication date, and no renewal of its copyright was checked.

In 2003, 20th Century Fox and Legend Films released a colorized version titled A Christmas Wish, with a Terry Moore audio commentary on the DVD. Colorization and added commentary can carry their own copyright. A faithful copy of the black-and-white original adds none.

editorial:
The Great Rupert (1950) is an American family comedy produced by George Pal and directed by Irving Pichel, with Jimmy Durante, Tom Drake and Terry Moore. Rupert is an animated squirrel. It was distributed by Eagle-Lion Films and released in the United States on March 1, 1950. It is based on a story by Ted Allan that was also published as the children's book Willie the Squowse.

Wikipedia reports that the film entered the public domain in 1978, when its 28-year term lapsed without renewal. This dossier could not confirm that from the renewal records. Treat the print as unverified until you check the Catalog of Copyright Entries and the Copyright Office's public records yourself. Two other layers are open: the Willie the Squowse book, whose date and renewal status are unchecked, and the score. The 2003 colorized release from Fox and Legend Films, titled A Christmas Wish, may be protected separately, so use a black-and-white print.
faq: Is The Great Rupert free to use?

It is reported as being in the public domain since 1978, but this dossier did not verify that against the renewal records. The story, which also appeared as the book Willie the Squowse, and the score were not checked either. Check the 1977 to 1979 renewal records before relying on it.
Can I use the colorized A Christmas Wish version?
Not safely. The 2003 colorization released by Fox and Legend Films may carry its own copyright, as may its added commentary. Use a black-and-white copy of the original instead.
